Multithreading in eigencore's sparse kernels

Source: R/threads.R
eigencore-threads.Rd

eigencore parallelises its native sparse (CSC, dgCMatrix) operator applications with OpenMP: A^T X products (a gather per column), A X products (a gather over a cached CSR copy, or a scatter over cached per-thread row slabs for tall matrices with short rows), the centred and centred-scaled sparse operators, and the implicit normal operators A^T A / A A^T behind sparse svds() / svd_partial(). Every output entry is accumulated by one thread in the same order and with the same arithmetic as the serial loop, so sparse products are bitwise identical for any thread count. While such a solve runs, the Lanczos reorthogonalisation also uses these threads (see below): single-threaded BLAS calls on fixed blocks of rows, shared among the threads, whose results do not depend on the thread count either, so results computed with one and with several threads differ only by rounding, and results with 2, 4 or 8 threads agree exactly.

Options

eigencore.threads

Number of threads, read at the start of every native call. When unset, a default fixed at package load is used: 1 under R CMD check (_R_CHECK_PACKAGE_NAME_ set) or when _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ is set (CRAN's core limit); otherwise the first value of OMP_NUM_THREADS when set; otherwise the number of processors available to OpenMP (respecting the CPU affinity mask), further limited to the physical cores (parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)) and to the cgroup CPU quota of a container, and capped at 8. Builds without OpenMP (for example Apple clang without libomp) always use one thread.

eigencore.adaptive_threads

TRUE (default) or FALSE. While enabled, eigencore watches the parallel efficiency of its own OpenMP regions and lowers the number of threads it actually uses when the machine is oversubscribed (see below). FALSE always uses eigencore.threads threads, as in eigencore 1.3.0.

eigencore.csr_cache_mb

Memory cap in MB (default 4096) for the per-operator CSR copy or row slabs (about 12 bytes per nonzero) that the parallel A X builds once per solve. When the copy would be larger, A X stays serial for blocks of up to 10 columns.

eigencore.parallel_min_work

Minimum work per thread of a parallel region (default 65536), in multiply-add units: a sparse product counts 4 units per nonzero and right-hand side, the reorthogonalisation 1 per basis entry and column. A region gets at most floor(work / eigencore.parallel_min_work) threads and runs serially below two, so small products (a 20000 x 20000 matrix with 3 nonzeros per row, about 60 microseconds) use few threads or one: they cannot gain from more and, when any core is busy, every join waits for the slowest team member. Like the adaptive thread count it only changes how many threads run a region, never the result. 0 lets every region use all threads; Inf keeps eigencore's own kernels serial. inst/benchmarks/bench-parallel-threshold.R measures the crossover on a machine.

Busy machines

OpenMP runtimes keep idle team threads spinning for a while (libgomp's default OMP_WAIT_POLICY), which is fast on idle cores. When other processes occupy the cores, every fork, join and barrier of a parallel region instead waits a scheduler time slice for a team member that is not running, and eigencore 1.3.0's short sparse kernels became 10-80 times slower with 4 threads than with 1. eigencore therefore times each parallel region: when a region takes longer than the master thread's share of the work times the team size (i.e. longer than running it serially would have), twice in a row, the team is halved, and a larger team is tried again after a pause that grows (0.25 s to 4 s) while the machine stays busy. Only the number of threads in a region changes; the algorithm and the work partition that determine rounding are chosen from eigencore.threads, so results do not depend on the machine load. The wait policy itself cannot be changed from a package (R loads the OpenMP runtime at start-up); on machines that are routinely oversubscribed, setting OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive in the environment before starting R also removes the spinning. A multithreaded OpenBLAS (pthreads build) spins the same way in its own dense calls (including those made between eigencore's native calls and by CHOLMOD); eigencore does not change it on its own because OpenBLAS results depend on its thread count, so on a busy machine also limit it (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, or RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1)).

Interaction with a multithreaded BLAS

OpenBLAS (pthreads build) and FlexiBLAS keep idle worker threads spinning after each call; OpenMP threads started meanwhile would compete with them for cores. When eigencore.threads is above one, a native sparse solve (for example eigs_sym(), svds() or svd_partial() on a dgCMatrix) therefore switches such a BLAS to one thread at its first sparse product (also when that product is too small to run in parallel) for the rest of that call and restores the previous setting when the call returns (or fails); its reorthogonalisation then runs on eigencore's threads. Sparse products applied one at a time from R-level operators (for example inside a matrix-free center() solve) stay serial while such a BLAS is multithreaded, so the surrounding BLAS work keeps its threads. An OpenMP-built OpenBLAS shares eigencore's thread pool; MKL, BLIS and other libraries are not changed. With those, or when running several R workers in parallel, consider options(eigencore.threads = 1) or limiting the BLAS threads (for example with RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads()).

Examples

old <- options(eigencore.threads = 1)
getOption("eigencore.threads")
#> [1] 1
options(old)
